extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, patent attorneys and law students (Australia-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for what makes an invention patentable under the Patents Act 1990 (Cth) and the procedural/content requirements for Australian patent applications. Covers subject-matter, novelty, inventive step, usefulness, secret use, specification/claim requirements, prosecution timelines, and international filing options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of manufacture (patentable subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be a 'manner of manufacture' within the meaning of the Statute of Monopolies (s 18 of the Patents Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concept is dynamic and flexible (NRDC). The invention must be a vendible product or process that produces an artificially produced state of affairs and have economic significance (industrial, commercial or trading character). It cannot be a mere discovery, idea, scientific theory or law of nature. The inquiry is purposive and should accommodate technological developments; not interpreted literally. Also note statutory exclusions (e.g., contrary to law, harmful to trade).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express exclusions / non-patentable subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories of subject matter are expressly considered not patentable under the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes human beings and biological processes for their generation, plants and animals (for innovation patents), products contrary to law, and mere mixtures. TRIPS-based exclusions are also relevant (e.g., protecting human/animal/plant life or avoiding serious prejudice to the environment). Examples: methods of in vitro fertilisation are excluded; specific statutory provisions cited (s 18(2),(3) etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter — computer software
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer software can be patentable where it produces a commercially useful and concrete result beyond a mere algorithm or mathematical formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (IBM, CCOM) show software that applies an algorithm to produce an improved, commercially useful result (e.g., improved graphics) can be patentable. Ordinary algorithms that merely 'computerize' another task are not patentable (Rokt). Emphasis on application to produce tangible/commercial effect rather than abstract algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter — business methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Business methods may be patentable only if they produce a concrete physical effect or manifestation — mere schemes or abstract ideas are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Street suggested openness to business-method patents, but Australian authorities (Grant v Commissioner) introduced a 'physicality' requirement: the invention must involve a concrete, tangible, physical or observable effect/manifestation or transformation. Legal advice, schemes, or mere intellectual information are not manners of manufacture. Case examples: State Street (US), Welcome Real-Time (persuasive), Grant (physicality requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter — biotechnology
rubrics_metrics.description: Biotechnology inventions may be patentable when they are non-naturally occurring manufactures or products of human ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diamond v Chakrabarty illustrates that genetically modified organisms or compositions that do not occur in nature and are produced by human intervention may qualify as patentable subject matter ('anything under the sun made by man'). Emphasises non-naturally occurring, human-made products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter — medical treatments (treating the human body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of medical treatment are not excluded from patentable subject matter and can be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apotex v Sanofi-Aventis (HCA majority) confirms methods of medical treatment can be patentable. Policy debates exist (access vs incentive), but medical-use method claims may be within scope of patentability; infringement and s117 (contributory infringement) issues remain relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter — genes and isolated genetic material
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentability of genes/isolated nucleic acids is constrained; chemical isolation of genes may not be patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D'Arcy v Myriad Genetics held that chemical isolation of nucleic acid sequences (BRCA1) was not patentable subject matter in that context. The page identifies gene-isolation as a contentious area and gives court outcome as a guiding example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (requirement that the invention be new)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be new: it must not have been disclosed to the public before the priority date when compared with the prior art base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is required by ss 18(1)(b)(i), 18(1A)(b)(i) and 7(1). The prior art base includes worldwide documents and acts. The reverse infringement test (Meyers Taylor) is a key test: the prior art must disclose all essential features of the claimed invention. 'Mosaicking' prior art is disfavoured, though reading documents together is permissible if incorporation by reference or plainly intended. Self-disclosure to public destroys novelty unless within the statutory grace period or confidential disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority date
rubrics_metrics.description: The priority date is the date at which novelty and inventive step are assessed against the prior art base — usually the filing date of the application (or provisional application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a provisional application can establish an earlier priority date provided the provisional discloses the invention clearly and completely enough for a person skilled in the art to perform it (s 43(2A)(b), reg.3.13C, s40(1)). A complete application must follow within 12 months for the provisional to secure priority. Paris Convention and PCT filings can also affect priority dates in multiple jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art base (scope of comparison for novelty/inventiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art base consists of publicly available information (documents or acts) anywhere in the world as of the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically confined to Australian disclosures, but after the Patents Amendment Act 2001 the prior art base is worldwide. Prior art must disclose all essential features (reverse infringement test). Certain types of disclosure may be disregarded under s 24 if a complete application is filed within 12 months (grace provisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disregarding certain types of public information (s 24 / grace period)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain public disclosures by the inventor or related persons can be disregarded for novelty and inventive step if a complete application is filed within 12 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to inventor self-publishing, publications or exhibitions, reading of papers to learned societies, reasonable public trials (where public working is necessary), and disclosures made without the patentee's consent. Specifics and regulation detail are in the Patents Regulations 1991. There is also a 12-month grace period for secret use (with respect to filing a complete application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step (non-obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must involve an inventive step: it would not have been obvious to a person skilled in the relevant art in light of the common general knowledge before the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory references: ss 18(1)(b)(ii) and 7(2). The threshold is relatively low — 'if it would not have been obvious', 'scintilla of inventiveness' may suffice. Must avoid hindsight. Identify person skilled in the art (hypothetical non-inventive worker; can be a team). Common general knowledge is background accepted knowledge of the technical community. Practical approach (Dura-Post): compare claim-by-claim with prior disclosures, identify variations, and decide whether variations make a substantial contribution to the invention. Determination is fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness / utility (s 7A)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be useful: the complete specification must disclose a specific, substantial and credible use for the invention, and disclose it sufficiently for a person skilled in the art to appreciate that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raising the Bar (2012) amendments inserted s 7A defining 'useful' as requiring a specific, substantial and credible use disclosed in the complete specification, and sufficient disclosure so the skilled person can appreciate that use. This is a stricter test than pre-2012 where utility was met by showing the invention worked as claimed; commercial viability is not required but specificity is. Note US practice differs (utility not examined pre-grant in the same way).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on secret use
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must not have been secretly used before the priority date; secret commercial use can invalidate a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret use is treated separately from public use; it prohibits extending monopoly by commercial exploitation before priority. s 9 lists uses not considered secret (reasonable trial/experiment, confidential disclosures, non-commercial uses, Commonwealth use). A 12-month grace period may apply for secret use when filing a complete application. Case example (Azuko v Old Digger): even one instance of commercial benefit (production/orders) can indicate commercial use rather than mere trial; facts matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification / description requirements (provisional and complete specifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent specification must disclose the invention clearly and completely enough for a person skilled in the relevant art to perform it; the complete specification must disclose the best known method and end with claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional specification must be clear and complete enough for performance by the skilled person. Complete specification (s 40) must disclose the invention sufficiently, disclose the best method known to the applicant, and conclude with claims. The complete specification must enable the specific, substantial and credible use (post-Raising the Bar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims content and formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the scope of monopoly and must be clear, succinct, supported by the specification, and relate to one invention only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: s 40(3)-(4) require claims to be clear and succinct and supported by matter disclosed in the specification; claims must not be broader than the contribution to the art described. Each claim is considered on its own merits (invalidity of one claim does not necessarily invalidate others). Claims must relate to one invention only. Aim is to prevent claims obtaining monopoly beyond the disclosed contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be given a purposive construction and construed according to ordinary principles of written documents, read in light of the specification and common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not import limitations from the body of the specification that are not reproduced in the claim. Read the specification as a whole; body of specification can qualify or define expressions in a claim where appropriate. If claim language is ambiguous, it is permissible to resort to the body of the specification for clarification. The specification must be construed in light of common general knowledge extant before the priority date. Purposive (not purely literal) construction applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent application process and procedural timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural steps and statutory time limits for filing, examination, prosecution, publication, opposition and grant in Australia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optional provisional filing creates priority date; if provisional filed, complete application must be filed within 12 months. Filing a complete application sets the filing date; application becomes open to public inspection (OPI) 18 months after priority date. Examination must be requested within 5 years of lodging a complete application. Applicants typically have 21 months to address examiner objections; re-examination may occur at Registrar's discretion. Acceptance may be appealed to the Federal Court; once accepted the application is open to public inspection and, after grant, infringement and revocation proceedings may follow. Opposition to grant can occur on grounds set out in s 59.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territoriality and international patent protection (PCT / Paris Convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent grants rights only within the territory of the granting country; overseas protection requires separate filings or international procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Australian patent gives monopoly in Australia only (Norbert Steinhardt v Meth). To protect inventions abroad, applicants may file in each desired country or use the PCT (WIPO) or Paris Convention to secure priority and simplify multiple filings. A PCT application facilitates filing in many countries but will result in national/regional phases subject to each jurisdiction's examination standards. Paris Convention permits later national filings without destroying novelty when relying on an earlier priority filing.
